Sygma Solutions Confidential · prepared for The Clancy Group Depotnet Review › Jack Blowers
← BackHomeThe findingsActionsAll inspectionsCoveragePerson by person

Jack Blowers

Clancy’s SE Water RM contract (Contract Manager: Stephen Jupe) · 83 reviews filed over ~13 months · 9 inspection PDFs read in full

New to this? The kit, the software and the form – explained in one minute
The CAT and the Genny
The CAT (Cable Avoidance Tool) is the handheld scanner crews sweep over the ground to find buried cables and pipes before they dig. The Genny is its partner – a signal generator that puts a traceable signal onto a buried service so the CAT can follow it. Using both, properly and for long enough, is the main defence against damaging a buried service.
The five modes
The CAT scans in different modes, and each finds things the others miss: Power (live electricity cables), Radio (metal services re-radiating radio signals), Genny HF and Genny LF (following the Genny’s signal at two frequencies), and Avoidance (a combined sweep). A thorough locate uses all of them.
The usage data – “scan time”
Modern CATs log every second of use. The log uploads to software called C.A.T Manager, which shows exactly how long each person scanned, in which modes, on which days. It is objective evidence of whether the kit is really being used. The form never states the units of its scan-time answer, and the live C.A.T Manager screens show totals in hours:minutes:seconds. Figures on these pages are quoted exactly as the records hold them; wherever a conclusion depends on a figure, it holds under any reading of the units. When a page here says a review recorded “00:13”, that is the scan time the reviewer read off this data and wrote on the form.
Depotnet and the review form
Depotnet is the inspection platform used by The Clancy Group – the utility contractor whose supervisors and crews these pages review. Sygma Solutions is the outside damage-prevention specialist doing the reviewing. The form this whole section is about – the “GENNY & CAT usage performance record” – is a supervisor sitting down regularly with a crew’s usage data: how long did they scan, which modes, is anything wrong. For each mode the form asks “Are there any actions relating to…?” Answering Yes creates an action – a recorded to-do with an owner, a due date and a close date. Answering No closes the subject.
“Closed in the same second”
Depotnet stamps the moment an action is created and the moment it is closed. When the two stamps are identical, the action was raised and marked resolved in one step – it never existed as a live piece of follow-up work.
Operative, plant number, contract labels
An operative is a member of the site crew – the person a review is about. A plant number is the company’s asset tag for one physical piece of kit; each CAT and each Genny has its own, so records naming the same number as two different instruments cannot both be right. Labels like “SE Water RM” or “SW7003” are Clancy’s client-contract names and codes exactly as Depotnet records them.

Who this is and what we read

Jack Blowers is a supervisor on the SE Water RM contract and, by volume, one of the biggest users of the Genny & CAT review form in the business – 83 reviews filed in about thirteen months. The job of these reviews: sit down with each crew’s scanner data and record, on a Depotnet form, how long they scanned, in which modes, and whether anything needs fixing.

We read every sampled review document in full – every page, every answer – alongside the full list of reviews filed and the business-wide actions data. Every finding cites the document it comes from, and the “To be fair” section is deliberate: the strongest honest case for the other side, not decoration.

The short version: the reviews happen on a real monthly rhythm and the data genuinely gets read – but the only standard ever applied is time on the clock, the old fixed scan-time target – officially abolished – lives on in writing, and the one set of formal actions ever raised was empty and closed in a single batch.

{{my_reviews}}
reviews filed – Depotnet’s broken scoring stamps every one “0% / Not Acceptable” (see overview, finding 1)
5.0 min
median gap between same-day submissions (shortest: 6 seconds)
100%
of sampled records done at the yard, not on site
“strive for 2”
the stopwatch target, coached in writing

Outline summary

Jack runs a genuine monthly review cadence – the same operatives come back round every ~30 days, and Jack does read the device data. The problem is what happens next. Across these records, the quality bar is time on the clock and nothing else: coaching, praise and criticism are all expressed as stopwatch targets, and the old fixed-duration target (once a “90 seconds per mode” rule, officially abolished because it taught people to watch the clock instead of the ground) lives on in writing, inflated to “strive for 2” minutes per mode. The fields headed Attitudes, Behaviours and Culture contain duration arithmetic, not observations of people.

When the record and the verdict disagree, the verdict wins: one review names a genny-mode deficiency and still answers “No” to both genny action questions. And the one time formal actions were raised – four modes flagged on a 02:47 scan – every action was an empty shell: no corrective measure, no comment, no due date, all four closed in the same minute four days later.

Concerns

  1. He coaches the stopwatch, in writing, in the audit system – “mildly acceptable usage. need another 40secs on each mode”, “over a minute each mode, need to strive for 2”, “minimum of 1minute each mode” recorded under Behaviours. The review layer that should catch stopwatch scanning is enforcing it.Evidence: 130478, 133004, 143511
  2. A named deficiency, and the action boxes still say No – 144693 writes “needs more time spent on genny mode on the cat” in two fields – and answers “No” to both genny action questions. Nothing was tracked.Evidence: 144693
  3. His only actioned record is four empty shells, batch-closed in one minute – 175937 (scan 02:47) raised actions on four modes – every one with a blank corrective measure, blank comments, no due date, all four closed at exactly 17:02 on 19/12/2025.Evidence: 175937
  4. The whole register is desk-batched at the yard – All 83 records are at yard locations, fired in bursts with a median 5 minutes between submissions (minimum 6 seconds); 207175 and 207431 share an identical usage window and identical free text, submitted a day apart.Evidence: register export; 207175, 207431
  5. The kit can’t be traced and the calibration field means nothing – Equipment (“plant”) numbers are placeholders in 6 of 9 records – “subby” (slang for subcontractor) and “GENNY SUBBIE”; on three records the “calibration date” equals the submission date, on others it’s months in the future – the same field means two different things on one form (207431).Evidence: 143511, 144693, 169533, 196212, 207175, 207431
  6. The bar drifts and declines pass silently – In July 2025, ~1:10 per mode was “mildly acceptable”; six weeks later “minimum of 1minute each mode” passed with zero actions. Scan figures falling from review to review (09:17→06:55; 05:59→04:58) draw no comment.Evidence: 130478 vs 143511; 196212→207175; 143511→169533
  7. Signature boxes are blank in every sampled record – The same empty signature images recur byte-for-byte (matching file hashes) – no operative has signed any sampled review.Evidence: all sampled PDFs

The register, seen live

To be fair

  • 175937 proves Jack will flag a colleague when the data is poor – the worst scan in the sample triggered actions on four modes, correctly leaving Radio alone. The failure is the empty follow-through, not the willingness.
  • 130478 is honest, quantified grading – “mildly acceptable” with a concrete target, not a wave-through.
  • 133004 quotes distinct per-mode figures – the device data genuinely gets opened, at mode level.
  • The monthly cadence is real: Andy Lovelock was reviewed four times across a year on consecutive ~30-day windows, and that operative’s trajectory did improve.
  • Later records attach photo evidence, and every record works through all five per-mode questions individually.

Sampled live from Depotnet by Pete Ashcroft, 30 July 2026, with full-document analysis of every exported PDF. Source documents, registers and starred exhibits are filed in Drive: depotnet-inspection-reviews. Scan-time figures are quoted exactly as the form records them (mm:ss, matching the C.A.T Manager totals seen live on screen); the form itself never states units – but whether a figure is read as minutes:seconds or as hours:minutes, the findings stand.

Who this is and what we read

Anthony Ellis is a supervisor on the Southern Water RM contract, and appears as both inspector and supervisor on every review sampled. The job of these reviews: sit down with each crew’s scanner data and record, on a Depotnet form, how long they scanned, in which modes, and whether anything needs fixing.

We read every sampled review document in full – every page, every answer – alongside the full list of reviews filed and the business-wide actions data. Every finding cites the document it comes from, and the “To be fair” section is deliberate: the strongest honest case for the other side, not decoration.

The short version: the 2025 reviews looked like real reviews; in 2026 the recorded scan answers collapsed 25-fold and every review still passed; the live device data shows single continuous presses standing in for whole modes, and the thing being praised is the dashboard’s colour, not anything a person did.

30 / 30
per-mode action questions answered “No” across all six records
00:07
a full day’s scanning, reviewed and passed
2:22
Genny total on record 202228 – matched a single continuous button press on screen
25×
collapse in scan figures between the 2025 and 2026 reviews

Outline summary

Anthony’s 2025 reviews look like reviews: same-day supervision, minutes of scanning, a comment praising real fieldwork (“Good mark ups”). His 2026 reviews are something else. The recorded scan answers collapse to 00:07, 00:13 and 00:08 for full usage days with all five modes ticked – and not one action is raised anywhere, ever. His own free text concedes the slide (“more times required as reds are slipping back”) while every action box on the same form says No.

C.A.T Manager shows each mode as a coloured tile – green when enough use was logged, red when not. What gets praised is that colour, not the person: “alot more green than last week”. The dashboard’s colour is the standard. Green closes the question – and red doesn’t open it. Reviewed live on screen, record 202228 showed a Genny total of 2:22 that matched a single continuous trigger press; the form for the same record says 00:08 and passes it.

Concerns

  1. Scan time collapsed 25-fold and nothing happened – 2025: 03:20, 03:55, 09:15. 2026: 00:07, 00:13, 00:08 – full usage days, all five modes ticked, zero actions raised in any record. The form never states its units; for 193761 the live data shows the “00:13” was a 13-minute-51 total made of 13 button presses averaging 63 seconds. Either way, nothing was questioned.Evidence: 136341, 142513, 171852 vs 179672, 193761, 202228
  2. His own comment admits the decline the form denies – 179672: “more times required as reds are slipping back” – written on a form whose five action questions all say No. The concession is in free text where nothing tracks it.Evidence: 179672
  3. The dashboard colour is the quality standard – “alot more green than last week” is the entire assessment of 12 days of usage. The praise is aimed at the platform’s colour coding, not at anything a person did.Evidence: 171852
  4. One long press, called good – Seen live on screen: 202228’s C.A.T Manager total showed Genny 2:22 in a single unbroken use – one held trigger turns the Genny tile green. The exported form records 00:08 and raises nothing. (Depotnet’s PDF export does not carry the uploaded screen photos; the live screen is the only place this is visible.)Evidence: 202228 + live Depotnet session 30/07/2026
  5. The paperwork isn’t where the work is – 202228’s GPS is in Brisbane, Australia against a “waterworks road” location; 136341 and 171852 share a GPS point ~40 miles from the stated site. Reviews of single days are submitted 7–18 days late.Evidence: 202228, 136341, 171852, 179672
  6. Compliance answers for modes never used – 142513 answers “Are there any actions relating to Genny HF? – No” for a session in which Genny HF was never used.Evidence: 142513

To be fair

  • 136341 is what good looks like here: usage and review on the same day, and “Good mark ups” praises a concrete field behaviour.
  • His equipment records are the tidiest in the sample – consistent plant numbers, in-date calibrations across successive reviews.
  • He did notice the decline (“reds are slipping back”) – the failing is that the system let it stay as a comment.
  • Photos attached on four of six records; 171852 reviews a proper multi-day window, the right shape for a usage review.

Who this is and what we read

Brett Ward is a supervisor on the Anglian Water contract, reviewing IMR Reactive and Northfield Utilities crews. The job of these reviews: sit down with each crew’s scanner data and record, on a Depotnet form, how long they scanned, in which modes, and whether anything needs fixing.

We read every sampled review document in full – every page, every answer – alongside the full list of reviews filed and the business-wide actions data. Every finding cites the document it comes from, and the “To be fair” section is deliberate: the strongest honest case for the other side, not decoration.

The short version: the best reviewing in the whole sample – real failures found, documented and corrected in person – undone by a system where actions get closed the same day they are raised, sometimes within minutes.

2
genuine defects found and formally actioned – the most in the sample
17 min
from raising an avoidance defect to closing it
6 / 7
reviews done the same day as the usage – the freshest in the sample
7 / 7
records where Behaviours is the single word “good”

Outline summary

Brett is the strongest reviewer in the sample. Six of seven reviews happen the same day as the work, scan times are recorded to the second and differ every time, and Brett has done what almost nobody else in the sample has: found real failures and written them down. He caught a crew re-attending an ongoing job without re-scanning, and another crew that never used avoidance mode at all – both raised as formal actions with named correctives.

Then the system lets the work down. The re-scan action was closed 17 minutes after it was raised, on the same form that still says the team “generally have a good commitment to scanning”. The avoidance action closed the same evening. A defect that lives less than an hour never changes anything. And underneath the good work, the same pattern as everywhere else: the form’s Behaviours box says just “good” on all seven records (Culture likewise on all six that ask it), the praise field has never been used, and one record praises the crew for time spent – “team scanned for just over 10mins” – on a form that itself says 12:27.

Concerns

  1. Actions never outlive the visit – 149239’s re-scan failure: raised 13:12, closed 13:29 – 17 minutes. 192247’s missed avoidance mode: raised and closed the same day. Both correctives are conversations; neither was ever verified afterwards.Evidence: 149239, 192247
  2. A defect and its contradiction on one form – 149239 documents that the crew did not re-scan an ongoing excavation – and closes with “team generally have a good commitment to scanning”.Evidence: 149239
  3. Praise aimed at the clock – 146319: “time spent well scanning, team scanned for just over 10mins” – duration as the virtue, on a form that records 12:27. The record contradicts itself and praises the number anyway.Evidence: 146319
  4. Improvement asks that never become actions – 150411 notes “more markings up outside the excavation” – an ask – with all five action questions No.Evidence: 150411
  5. Boilerplate ratings and phantom photos – Behaviours = “good” in 7/7; Areas of praise blank in 7/7; two records answer Yes to “additional comments or photos” and contain neither; late-evening submissions at 21:05 and 21:04 on consecutive days point to end-of-day batching.Evidence: 150411, 156962, 157339
  6. Kit records that don’t hold still – The same Genny carries two calibration dates nine days apart; the CAT appears as cl3644 and CL3664 with the same calibration date – transposed digits for the same unit.Evidence: 146319 vs 149239

To be fair

  • The only inspector who re-audited a crew nine days after a clean review and caught a real failure the second time (146319 → 149239).
  • 192247 is internally honest end to end: the mode list omits avoidance, matching the defect raised – the form wasn’t sanitised.
  • Real behavioural observation exists here: “happy to scan every 150mm whilst going down the excavation”, “straight out the van, scanning and marking up”.
  • Six of seven reviews are same-day; the one that isn’t declares and explains the gap, and Brett went back and watched the team leader scan correctly.
  • Scan times recorded to the second, different every time – consistent with genuinely timing rather than pasting.

Who this is and what we read

Adam Bailey is a supervisor on the Anglian Water Recycling contract – 44 reviews filed in the period. The job of these reviews: sit down with each crew’s scanner data and record, on a Depotnet form, how long they scanned, in which modes, and whether anything needs fixing.

We read every sampled review document in full – every page, every answer – alongside the full list of reviews filed and the business-wide actions data. Every finding cites the document it comes from, and the “To be fair” section is deliberate: the strongest honest case for the other side, not decoration.

The short version: the clearest proof in the sample that the data is looked at but cannot be read: scan totals of 13 seconds, 12 seconds and 2 seconds all passed with nothing raised, and the 12-second one was praised in writing as “a good amount”.

00:02
scan total for a five-day window – passed, no actions
“good amount”
the verdict written on a 00:12 scan total
{{my_reviews}}

18

Outline summary

Adam’s records are the clearest proof in the sample that the data is looked at and cannot be read. He opens the download, reads the number off it, writes it on the form – 00:13 for a six-day window, 00:12, 00:02 for a five-day window – and passes every one with “No” in all five action boxes. On the 00:12 the verdict is there in Adam’s own words: “good amount of cat and Jenny [sic] used”. The form asked the right question. The answer was two seconds. And the box that mattered said No.

Where written comments exist at all, it praises the numbers as numbers – “good times using modes”, “good times on download” – and the October→December trend (00:13 → 00:12 → 00:02) is downward with no reaction. The one action raised (a crew not using Genny HF) was honest – and Adam closed it personally the next morning on the words “Going forward this will be used”.

Concerns

  1. The starred trilogy: 00:13, 00:12, 00:02 – all passed – 165916: six-day window, 00:13, no actions. 169820: 00:12, “good amount of cat and Jenny used”, praise box ticked. 174865: five-day window, 00:02 – two seconds – no actions, and no operative named anywhere on the form.Evidence: 165916, 169820, 174865
  2. The praise is for the numbers themselves – “good times using modes” (22:39 over two days), “good times on download” – the download total is the thing being congratulated. Nothing about how anyone scanned.Evidence: 205554, 205555
  3. The trend was down and nobody reacted – His own records run 00:13 → 00:12 → 00:02 across October–December 2025. Three consecutive reviews, each thinner than the last, no comment in any of them.Evidence: 165916 → 169820 → 174865
  4. Batch paperwork dressed as supervision – 205554 and 205555 have consecutive record IDs but were submitted four days apart in reverse order – two forms made in one sitting, one back-filled 8–9 days after the usage. 205554’s GPS is ~40 km from its stated yard.Evidence: 205554, 205555
  5. The one action closed itself on a promise – 207228 caught Genny HF not being used – honestly recorded. Adam owned the action and closed it the next morning: corrective measure “Going forward this will be used”. No verification; due date a week away.Evidence: 207228
  6. Records that can’t be traced – 174865 names no operative and locates itself as “NN17, England”; 161078’s job reference is “12345” and its calibration dates sit three months before submission; the same operative appears under two spellings and two employment statuses across the year.Evidence: 174865, 161078, 169820 vs 189694

To be fair

  • 207228 is genuine supervision: Adam spotted Genny HF not being used, recorded the defect, and the modes-used list honestly omits HF – the failure is the next-morning self-closure, not the catch.
  • 174865 contains real calibration management: “Genny is being swapped out Monday 8/12/25” – the exact day its calibration fell due. Known, planned, acted on.
  • Most reviews are close to the work – several same-day or final-day-of-window.
  • He evidences instinctively: 18 photos across five records, and kit is consistently traceable per crew across months.
  • He follows crews across live jobs, yard sessions and subcontract gangs – not just easy targets.

Wayne Dodd

Clancy’s Southern Water contracts (RM / SW7003) · 9 inspection PDFs read in full · reviews submitted in desk batches (3 in 14 minutes; 2 in 6 minutes)

New to this? The kit, the software and the form – explained in one minute
The CAT and the Genny
The CAT (Cable Avoidance Tool) is the handheld scanner crews sweep over the ground to find buried cables and pipes before they dig. The Genny is its partner – a signal generator that puts a traceable signal onto a buried service so the CAT can follow it. Using both, properly and for long enough, is the main defence against damaging a buried service.
The five modes
The CAT scans in different modes, and each finds things the others miss: Power (live electricity cables), Radio (metal services re-radiating radio signals), Genny HF and Genny LF (following the Genny’s signal at two frequencies), and Avoidance (a combined sweep). A thorough locate uses all of them.
The usage data – “scan time”
Modern CATs log every second of use. The log uploads to software called C.A.T Manager, which shows exactly how long each person scanned, in which modes, on which days. It is objective evidence of whether the kit is really being used. The form never states the units of its scan-time answer, and the live C.A.T Manager screens show totals in hours:minutes:seconds. Figures on these pages are quoted exactly as the records hold them; wherever a conclusion depends on a figure, it holds under any reading of the units. When a page here says a review recorded “00:13”, that is the scan time the reviewer read off this data and wrote on the form.
Depotnet and the review form
Depotnet is the inspection platform used by The Clancy Group – the utility contractor whose supervisors and crews these pages review. Sygma Solutions is the outside damage-prevention specialist doing the reviewing. The form this whole section is about – the “GENNY & CAT usage performance record” – is a supervisor sitting down regularly with a crew’s usage data: how long did they scan, which modes, is anything wrong. For each mode the form asks “Are there any actions relating to…?” Answering Yes creates an action – a recorded to-do with an owner, a due date and a close date. Answering No closes the subject.
“Closed in the same second”
Depotnet stamps the moment an action is created and the moment it is closed. When the two stamps are identical, the action was raised and marked resolved in one step – it never existed as a live piece of follow-up work.
Operative, plant number, contract labels
An operative is a member of the site crew – the person a review is about. A plant number is the company’s asset tag for one physical piece of kit; each CAT and each Genny has its own, so records naming the same number as two different instruments cannot both be right. Labels like “SE Water RM” or “SW7003” are Clancy’s client-contract names and codes exactly as Depotnet records them.

Who this is and what we read

Wayne Dodd is a supervisor on the Southern Water contracts, and one of the few inspectors in the business who has formally actioned low scan time – the exact behaviour these reviews exist to catch. The job of these reviews: sit down with each crew’s scanner data and record, on a Depotnet form, how long they scanned, in which modes, and whether anything needs fixing.

We read every sampled review document in full – every page, every answer – alongside the full list of reviews filed and the business-wide actions data. Every finding cites the document it comes from, and the “To be fair” section is deliberate: the strongest honest case for the other side, not decoration.

The short version: the standard collapsed six-fold inside a month – a three-minute scan was formally actioned in early July, and another days after – then 31-second scans passed without comment four weeks on; both actions were closed by their own raiser within minutes, and one photo of a monitor served as the evidence on three separate reviews.

03:13 → 00:31
what got actioned in early July vs what passed untouched four weeks later
6 min
from an action being raised to being closed – by the same person
3
records carrying the byte-identical photo of the same monitor
08:55
the same scan-time answer on two unrelated records filed 14 minutes apart

Outline summary

Wayne is, on paper, one of the few inspectors who acts on the data: in early July Wayne raised formal “low usage time” actions on scans of 03:13 and 03:04. Then both actions were closed by the person who raised them – one six minutes after submission, one three minutes – with correctives that read “Increse time” [sic] and “Increase slightly”. And four weeks later the same inspector passed 00:31, 00:31 and 00:32 – a sixth of what had been actioned weeks earlier – without a word, two of them against two-day usage windows.

The mechanics point to a desk, not a trench: three records submitted in 14 minutes covering different crews, sites and days; two more in 6 minutes at neighbouring addresses; the same 08:55 scan answer on two unrelated records; and one photo of a monitor, byte-identical, attached to three separate performance records. Kit identities don’t survive either – two plant numbers swap Genny/CAT roles between records, and one unit carries three calibration dates inside eight days, the last being exactly submission-date-plus-one-year.

Concerns

  1. The bar collapsed six-fold in four weeks – 01/07: 03:13 formally actioned as “Low usage in time”. 14/07: 03:04 actioned. 29–30/07: 00:31, 00:31 and 00:32 pass with zero actions four weeks later – two of them for two-day windows.Evidence: 202763, 204794 vs 207523, 207594, 207603
  2. Self-raised, self-owned, self-closed in minutes – 202763: submitted 13:57, action closed 14:03 – six minutes, a week before its due date. 204794: submitted 13:44, closed 13:47. Corrective measures: “Increse time”, “Increase slightly”. Nothing verified.Evidence: 202763, 204794
  3. One photo, three performance records – The identical image of a monitor (matching file hash) is attached to 207523, 207594 and 207603 – three separate reviews sharing one piece of evidence.Evidence: 207523, 207594, 207603
  4. Identical answers on unrelated records – 08:55 appears on 206259 and 206262 – different operatives, sites and kit, submitted 14 minutes apart. 00:31 appears twice six minutes apart, with 00:32 the next day.Evidence: 206259, 206262, 207523, 207594, 207603
  5. Desk batches, not site visits – Three reviews in 14 minutes on 22/07 (16:38, 16:47, 16:52) spanning different crews and usage days; two in 6 minutes on 29/07 at 70 and 74 Singlewell Rd.Evidence: 206259, 206260, 206262; 207523, 207594
  6. Kit records that contradict themselves – Plants 4890/4857 are Genny/CAT in one record and CAT/Genny eight days later; plant 5112 is a Genny, then a CAT, with three calibration dates in eight days – the last exactly one year after submission day. 202763 says “Genny out of date, swap over” while recording an in-date calibration; 206262’s two calibration dates both equal the inspection day.Evidence: 204794 vs 206259; 206260, 207523, 207603; 202763; 206262

To be fair

  • He is one of only three inspectors in the sample who ever raised a formal action, and the only one to action low scan time specifically – the exact behaviour this review exists to catch.
  • “Genny out of date, swap over” caught a real kit issue, and that unit never reappears – consistent with an actual swap.
  • Reviews are filed the same day to three days after the usage they cover, worst case five – no months-stale reviewing.
  • Every record has a photo, and the core fields (window, plant, calibration) are never blank.

Who this is and what we read

Justin Muircroft supervises AM Water subcontract crews on the Anglian Water contract – 42 reviews filed in the period. The job of these reviews: sit down with each crew’s scanner data and record, on a Depotnet form, how long they scanned, in which modes, and whether anything needs fixing.

Every finding cites the document it comes from, and the “To be fair” section is deliberate: the strongest honest case for the other side, not decoration.

The short version: the field the whole form is named for – how long did they scan? – contains a computer timestamp instead of a scan time on every sampled form, so scan length is literally unrecorded; and one signature photo was submitted, identical file for file, on two reviews five weeks apart.

4 / 4
records where the “How long did they scan for?” field holds a timestamp, not a duration
1 photo
signature reused byte-identically across two inspections, five weeks apart
20 / 20
per-mode action questions answered “No”
0
photos of anything, in any record – the form’s additional-photos question answered “No” every time

Outline summary

Justin’s four sampled records share a defect that undermines the entire exercise: the field the form is named for – “How long did they scan for?” – contains a millisecond-precision timestamp in every record, not a duration. Scan length is literally unrecorded in 100% of these reviews; in one record the “duration” is dated seventeen hours after the review was submitted. On top of that sit assertions the form cannot support: “Constant good scans”, with no scan data on the page.

The signatures are their own story. One signature photo appears byte-for-byte identical in two inspections five weeks apart – the same file resubmitted, which no genuine signing could produce. The others are scrawls photographed on whatever was nearby: marker pen on a wall, biro on the corner of a loose sheet. And in one record the Genny and the CAT – two different instruments – share a single identical plant number and calibration date.

Concerns

  1. Scan length is never actually recorded – All four records hold an ISO timestamp (e.g. “2026-04-15T08:04:27.349Z”) where a duration should be. 196067’s value post-dates its own submission by ~17 hours. No reviewer can ever verify scan time from these forms.Evidence: 190092, 196067, 199443, 205429
  2. One signature photo, two inspections – The same signature image (matching file hash) appears in 190092 (15 April) and 196067 (20 May) – same crew, five weeks apart. A signature cannot be produced byte-identically twice; it is one photo, resubmitted.Evidence: 190092, 196067
  3. Signatures on walls and paper corners – 205429’s signature is marker pen written on a wall; 199443’s is biro on the corner of a loose sheet – photographed as the formal sign-off of a safety-critical review.Evidence: 205429, 199443
  4. Praise the form cannot support – “Constant good scans” (190092), “Good usage on all modes” (199443) – written on forms that contain no scan duration at all. written in the form’s Attitudes/Behaviours/Culture boxes. All 20 action questions say No, and the form’s dedicated “Areas of praise” question is blank in all four.Evidence: 190092, 199443
  5. Two instruments, one identity – 205429 records the Genny and the CAT under the identical plant number with identical calibration dates – one asset record standing for two devices.Evidence: 205429
  6. No evidence of anything – “Do you have any additional Comments or Photos to upload?” – No, in all four records. Zero photographs of kit, site or screen anywhere in the sample.Evidence: 190092, 196067, 199443, 205429

To be fair

  • Three of four reviews were submitted the same day as the stated usage – the work is fresh, not months stale.
  • 196067 links performance to an equipment change (“usage improved since change of CAT”) – and the CAT’s plant number genuinely did change. That is real, equipment-aware observation.
  • He covers three different crews rather than re-reviewing one favourite gang, and payroll-style identification is present.
  • Nothing in the written comments praises durations or dashboard colours – the praise, though formulaic, is aimed at behaviour.

Andrew Laker is a supervisor on the Southern Water RM contract who runs the weekly usage reviews for around ten crews at a time. The job of these reviews: sit down with each crew’s scanner data and record, on a Depotnet form, how long they scanned, in which modes, and whether anything needs fixing.

We read every sampled review document in full – every page, every answer – alongside the full list of reviews filed and the business-wide actions data. The short version: ten crews’ reviews were completed in 35 minutes from one desk; the crews’ scan times varied twelve-fold, yet every answer was No, every praise box empty, and not one word was written anywhere across eleven documents.

10 in 35 min
crews reviewed in one sitting on 15 July – one GPS point for all of them
55 / 55

01:53 → 23:13

Outline summary

On the morning of 15 July 2026, Andrew reviewed ten crews in 35 minutes – one every three and a half minutes, all from effectively the same GPS point (Depotnet stamps a location on every submission). The inputs vary twelve-fold: one crew’s scan total for the six-day window is 01:53, another’s is 23:13. The outputs do not vary at all: every action question answered No, every praise field blank, and not one word of free text anywhere in eleven records. Each crew’s dashboard genuinely was opened – the plant numbers and figures differ – but what came back is a roll-call, not a review.

The supporting detail doesn’t survive contact either: the location field is blank in all eleven records; every photo is a phone shot of the C.A.T Manager screen on an office monitor; two different crews’ records carry the identical map image pinned at Horsham WTW (a water treatment works); two-man crews are signed off with a single scribble; and one plant number, cl4204, appears in three records covering the same week as three different instruments with three different calibration dates.

Concerns

  1. A 35-minute roll-call standing in for eleven reviews – Ten submissions between 09:27 and 10:02 on 15/07/2026, ~3.5 minutes each, one GPS point (Depotnet stamps a location on every submission). These are the “weekly usage performance records” for ten separate crews.Evidence: 204926–204954
  2. Inputs vary 12-fold; the verdict never moves – 01:53 (204926) to 23:13 (204940) for the identical six-day window – and 55 of 55 action questions are No. The extremes belong to the same review sitting, minutes apart, and neither drew a comment. The same operative holds both high outliers of the whole set (21:33 in June, 23:13 in July), unremarked.Evidence: 204926, 204940, 200543
  3. Zero words, eleven records – No free text exists anywhere in the set – no comments, no praise, no coaching. The only prose in every PDF is the Depotnet template’s own boilerplate.Evidence: 200543–204954
  4. Two crews, one identical map – 204944 (Jake Crockett) and 204952 (Ryan Byrne) carry the byte-identical map image pinned at Horsham WTW – two different crews’ “locations” are one copied artefact. The location field itself is blank in all 11 records.Evidence: 204944, 204952
  5. One plant number, three identities in one week – cl4204 is the CAT (cal 09/06/2027) in 204926, the Genny (cal 14/04/2027) in 204932, and the CAT again (cal 04/02/2027) in 204940 – three conflicting records of one unit inside the same usage week. At least two are wrong.Evidence: 204926, 204932, 204940
  6. Signatures that aren’t signatures – Two-operative crews carry one signature scribble for both people (204929, 204932); other “signatures” are a single curved stroke or a near-flat line.Evidence: 204929, 204932, 204949, 204952

To be fair

  • Each crew’s dashboard was individually opened – plant numbers and scan figures are distinct per record, so this is a real weekly data check, done badly, rather than fabrication.
  • Every calibration in all 11 records is in date, and operative payroll numbers are present in five records.
  • The cadence is genuine and current: every window ends on the day of submission – the reviews cover the week just gone, weekly, with repeat coverage of the same operatives.
  • The dashboard-photo habit, for all its faults, evidences the data source for every single record.

findings.html:
Sygma Solutions Confidential · prepared for The Clancy Group Depotnet Review › The findings
← BackHomeThe findingsActionsAll inspectionsCoveragePerson by person

The findings

Nine points that hold the whole review together. Each one is computed from Depotnet’s own exports or read directly from the inspection documents; the data pages and person pages carry the full evidence.

What the whole sample says

1 · The scoring layer has never functioned – definitively. Every completed inspection of this type in the entire business – all {{inspections}} of them, 170 inspectors, 22 contracts, thirteen and a half months – is 0 points, 0%, “Not Acceptable”. Not one exception. The score is a dead default, and nobody upstream can have been reading it.

2 · The data is looked at – and cannot be read. The form asks the right question (“How long did they scan for?”) and the answer is transcribed faithfully: 00:13, 00:12, 00:07, 00:02. Then the box that matters says No. One reviewer read 00:12 off the download and wrote “good amount of cat and Jenny used”.

3 · Duration is the only lens – and the review layer coaches the stopwatch. Praise and criticism alike aim at the clock: “strive for 2” [minutes], “need another 40secs on each mode”, “good times on download”. The check that should catch stopwatch scanning is enforcing it, in writing, in the audit system.

4 · Both extremes pass identically. Two seconds and twenty-three minutes get the same verdict: all five action boxes No. The number on the form has no effect on the outcome – which means the review, as performed, measures nothing.

5 · The few real actions die in minutes. Nine action answers of “Yes” exist in the entire sample. Of the formal actions raised, nearly all were closed by the person who raised them, within 3–17 minutes, several on a promise (“Going forward this will be used”) with blank correctives and no verification.

6 · The structured fields are dead. “Areas of praise”: blank in effectively every record in the sample. Photo captions: blank on every one of the ~50 uploaded photos. Attitudes / Behaviours / Culture: duration arithmetic, site descriptions, or the word “good”.

7 · The paperwork is done at desks. Ten reviews in 35 minutes from one GPS point; three in 14 minutes; two in 6; late-evening batches; a review whose own GPS sits in Brisbane, Australia; identical scan answers and identical photos shared across “independent” records.

8 · Equipment identity doesn’t hold. Plant numbers swap between Genny and CAT roles, one number serves three instruments in a week, calibration dates equal “today” on some forms and “due date” on others – the calibration field cannot be relied on to mean anything.

9 · And the instinct to do it right exists in-house. Real defects were found and honestly recorded – a crew that didn’t re-scan an ongoing dig, a crew that never used avoidance mode, low-time actions on exactly the behaviour that matters. The people are not the ceiling; the system that lets every action close itself in minutes is.

Why this matters: the case that better reviews reduce service damage stands on honest, readable records. This is the layer that should turn device data into knowledge – and on this evidence it is transcribing the data without being able to interpret it, while the scoring underneath has never worked. Every finding here is document-cited and re-checkable against the filed PDFs.

The actions register – the whole business, one year

Exported 30 July 2026: every action ever raised from this inspection type across the business – {{gc_actions}} action entries from the {{with_action}} inspections (of the {{inspections}} completed) that raised at least one action – 114 inspectors, 15 contracts, July 2025 to July 2026. So actions are raised at scale. Then the register shows what happens to them:

· {{same_second_pct}} of closed actions were closed in the same second they were raised (1,347 of 1,961). The median life of an action is zero minutes. Several inspectors run at 90–100% same-second; whether inspectors close instantly or the platform writes raise-and-close in one step, the result is the same – for two-thirds of everything raised, the register cannot show any action ever having an independent life.

· 92% of closed actions are owned by the inspector who raised them. Raise it, own it, close it – one person, one sitting.

· The corrective vocabulary is a conversation and a clock. The most common correctives, verbatim: “spoken to gang” (and its spellings), “use for longer”, “monitor”, “all good now”, “sorted”, “increase”. Across roughly two thousand corrective texts, “technique” appears zero times, “calibration” zero, “marking” zero, “sweep” once. Duration words (“more time”, “more usage”, “increase”, “low usage”, “seconds”, “minute”) appear ~900 times.

· Severity changes nothing. Only 33 entries in the year are Major Non-Conformance – 1.6% – and 14 of those closed in the same second too. One major reads “only 10 seconds of scans completed in power mode”; another records a team about to dig before a supervisor stepped in.

· Avoidance is the most-actioned mode (633 entries), then Genny HF (464) – the same modes the sampled records show being skipped.

To be fair here too: a handful of inspectors use the system as designed – one has zero same-second closures out of 41 rows and carries genuinely open actions today. The capability exists. The system neither requires nor rewards it.

The Actions Register – every action, charted → Completed Inspections – all {{inspections}}, find-rates, the zero-action 56 → Operative coverage – who gets reviewed, who’s forgotten →

Kept deliberately fair

Each page carries a “To be fair” section, and it is not decoration. Several inspectors show genuine, timely supervision; three found and documented real defects; one manages calibration properly. The consistent read across all seven is capability without a functioning system: nobody has ever shown them what the data means, nothing upstream reacts to what they write, and the score at the bottom has said “Not Acceptable” on every record for a year without anyone noticing. That is a system problem, and it is fixable.

Where this comes from, and how to read it

On 30 July 2026 Pete Ashcroft went through the review system end to end, live in Depotnet: seven supervisors’ review documents (Depotnet calls them “inspectors”) were exported and read line by line – 56 documents, every page, every answer – alongside Depotnet’s own business-wide exports: every completed review of this type ({{inspections}}), every action ever raised from one ({{gc_actions}}), and the per-operative coverage list. All source files are kept in Drive; every claim on these pages cites its document.

How to read this section: the numbered findings below are the whole story in nine points. The three data pages (buttons above) chart the business-wide picture. The seven name cards at the bottom go person by person, with the actual form pages on screen.

New to this? The kit, the software and the form – explained in one minute
The CAT and the Genny
The CAT (Cable Avoidance Tool) is the handheld scanner crews sweep over the ground to find buried cables and pipes before they dig. The Genny is its partner – a signal generator that puts a traceable signal onto a buried service so the CAT can follow it. Using both, properly and for long enough, is the main defence against damaging a buried service.
The five modes
The CAT scans in different modes, and each finds things the others miss: Power (live electricity cables), Radio (metal services re-radiating radio signals), Genny HF and Genny LF (following the Genny’s signal at two frequencies), and Avoidance (a combined sweep). A thorough locate uses all of them.
The usage data – “scan time”
Modern CATs log every second of use. The log uploads to software called C.A.T Manager, which shows exactly how long each person scanned, in which modes, on which days. It is objective evidence of whether the kit is really being used. Times on these pages are minutes:seconds – so “00:13” means thirteen seconds. When a page here says a review recorded “00:13”, that is the scan time the reviewer read off this data and wrote on the form.
Depotnet and the review form
Depotnet is the inspection platform used by The Clancy Group – the utility contractor whose supervisors and crews these pages review. Sygma Solutions is the outside damage-prevention specialist doing the reviewing. The form this whole section is about – the “GENNY & CAT usage performance record” – is a supervisor sitting down regularly with a crew’s usage data: how long did they scan, which modes, is anything wrong. For each mode the form asks “Are there any actions relating to…?” Answering Yes creates an action – a recorded to-do with an owner, a due date and a close date. Answering No closes the subject.
“Closed in the same second”
Depotnet stamps the moment an action is created and the moment it is closed. When the two stamps are identical, the action was raised and marked resolved in one step – it never existed as a live piece of follow-up work.
Operative, plant number, contract labels
An operative is a member of the site crew – the person a review is about. A plant number is the company’s asset tag for one physical piece of kit; each CAT and each Genny has its own, so records naming the same number as two different instruments cannot both be right. Labels like “SE Water RM” or “SW7003” are Clancy’s client-contract names and codes exactly as Depotnet records them.
